title: Your Chevron Hedge Works Only While Oil Spikes - Trefis
content: Our Nov 18 look at Chevron found the stock moving on its own. Chevron gained 2.3% from November 10 to November 17, while the S&P 500 lost 2.4%. For the full record, see Is Chevron Stock Increasing Your Market Risk? The next question is whether Chevron protects a portfolio when oil prices jump. The short answer is yes during the spike month, and usually no in the months after it. In the month of a spike, Chevron beat the market in 19 of 26 cases. Over the three months after a spike, it beat the market in only 9 of 25 cases. In an ordinary three-month stretch, it beats the market 48.6% of the time. The common view is that energy stocks jump when oil supply looks tight. The data agrees for the spike month itself. This piece looks at what came after. We set a rule in advance. A spike month is a calendar month in which USO, a fund built to follow oil prices, rose 10% or more. Since 2006, that happened in 26 months. Those months form 21 separate episodes. We compared Chevron with SPY, a fund that tracks the S&P 500. In the spike month, Chevron averaged a 7.7% gain. SPY averaged 2.1%. October 2026 was one of those months. USO rose 15.9%. Chevron rose 15.3%, while SPY slipped 0.91%. Since then, the move has reversed. From the Oct 30 close to Wednesday’s close, USO fell 19.4%. Chevron returned -11.9%, against -3.4% for SPY. Chevron has given back 11.9% since the end of October. If you own it mainly for its income, you may want income that does not rise and fall with the price of oil. Meanwhile, the Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3x the S&P 500’s, from 50 stocks with at least 10 straight years of dividends. See what it pays. Chevron closed at $205.88 on Wednesday, Nov 18. That was 4.7% below Tuesday’s close of $216.13. Part of the drop was the dividend. Wednesday was the ex-dividend date, the first day a buyer no longer gets the next payout. Counting the dividend, Chevron returned -4.0%. Other energy names and oil itself fell with it on Wednesday: Our data does not show why these stocks fell on Wednesday. Not usually. In the month after a spike, Chevron beat SPY in 11 of 25 cases, or 44%. In an ordinary one-month stretch, it beats SPY 49.4% of the time. Its median return that next month was -0.63%, against 1.3% for SPY. Over three months, the gap widens. Chevron beat SPY in 9 of 25 cases, or 36%. Its median three-month return was 0.40%, against 4.1% for SPY. October 2026 is left out of these counts because its windows are not complete. The table below shows how often each of three energy stocks beat SPY, in the spike month and after it. Source: Trefis analysis of Intrinio prices, May 2006 to October 2026. Prices are adjusted for splits and dividends. A spike month is a month when USO closed at least 10% above the prior month-end close. Chevron led the group in the spike month. It then had the weakest three-month record of the three. Think of a $1 million portfolio with 5% in Chevron and the rest in SPY. We compared it with a portfolio fully in SPY, held without changes. The Chevron slice changed the result this way: The range was wide. The best three-month case added $22,414. The worst cost $17,137. The record has clear exceptions. After December 2021, Chevron returned 40.2% over three months. SPY lost 4.6% over the same stretch. The opposite case is recent. March 2026 was the biggest USO month in the record, at 55.3%. Chevron rose 10.8% that month while SPY fell 4.9%. Over the next three months, Chevron lost about 19% while SPY gained 15.1%. Exxon Mobil held up better than Chevron over the three months after a spike. It beat SPY in 12 of 25 three-month windows. That is above its own normal rate of 42.4%. For a closer look at Exxon, see What Is Going On With Exxon Mobil Stock? The record shows a tendency, not a rule. We think a new oil spike could again lift Chevron during the spike itself. If history is a guide, it would not be a surprise if Chevron trailed the market over the following three months. December 2021 shows the pattern can break. The bigger question of how energy dividends compare with AI growth is in our piece Dividend Stocks Or AI Stocks: Which Fits Now? Our read: Chevron has protected a portfolio during an oil spike, not after it. Much of October’s gain is already gone. title: Is Chevron Stock Increasing Your Market Risk? - Trefis
content: Today’s big story: Anthropic IPO: Priced For 2031, Or 2036? Investors holding Chevron (CVX) alongside a broader index fund may have noticed the stock moving on its own. Chevron’s share price rose 1.5% from November 10 to November 17, 2026, while the S&P 500 lost 2.4%. A stock that detaches from the index changes how a bad market day affects a portfolio. So when the market falls, does Chevron fall with the rest of your money? On average, no: in the year to November 17, 2026, Chevron tended to move the opposite way to the index. On the average day the S&P 500 fell, a drop of 0.632%, a $10,000 holding in Chevron gained about $58. On the average day the index rose by 0.667%, that same holding lost about $25. Beta measures how far a stock moves for each 1% the index moves. Chevron’s beta was -0.51 over that year. Across all days, the stock tended to move about half as far as the index, in the opposite direction. It fell on the index’s three worst days, though: on November 5, 2026, when the S&P 500 fell 4.4%, Chevron fell 1.9%. It also fell 0.6% on each of the index’s next two worst days. The index fell 2.6% on June 5, 2026, and 2.1% on January 20, 2026. Chevron also exhibited wider swings on its own. The stock’s volatility, a measure of how widely the price swings over a year, was 24.6% over the past year, against 13.8% for the index. Chevron therefore pulled some broader market risk out of a portfolio, but it introduced larger price swings of its own. Chevron’s swings are likely to stay wide, because its earnings move with oil and fuel prices that management calls very volatile. On the October 30, 2026 call, management said oil traded as low as $68 and as high as $132 a barrel within the third quarter. It said adjusted upstream earnings, from producing oil and gas, fell from the second quarter. The causes were lower realized prices, lower volumes sold and unfavorable timing effects. Adjusted downstream earnings rose on higher refining margins. Management also expects refining margins to stay elevated in the short term, with 10% of the world’s refining capacity offline. Chevron’s pull against the market is less certain to last. Its correlation with the index, a score from -1 to 1 of how closely two prices move together, was -0.29 over the past year. That figure stood at 0.29 over the five years from November 2021, reflecting a loose tendency to move with the market rather than against it. Yes, by a little. Including dividends, Chevron returned 17.6% a year from November 9, 2021 to November 17, 2026. The S&P 500 returned 10.9% a year over the same dates. Its annual volatility over those five years was 25.4%, against 17.2% for the index. Chevron earned 0.693 of yearly return for each unit of swing, against 0.634 for the index. So Chevron’s swings have paid slightly better than the market’s. Management said Chevron has raised its dividend for 39 consecutive years. Chevron tended to slip slightly on the market’s good days and gain on its bad ones over the past year. Held beside an index fund, the stock has on average offset part of the market’s moves in both directions. It still fell on the index’s three worst days of the year. For investors who already own oil producers, refiners or an energy fund, buying Chevron adds more of that same bet on oil and fuel prices. Chevron’s refining margins are the measure to watch at its next report, expected in January 2027. Chevron’s return over those five years included a dividend that management keeps raising. Over the same four quarters, Marathon Petroleum grew revenue 31.2%, compared with 20.8% for Chevron. Yet its shares trade at just 7.7 times earnings. The extra price you pay for Chevron buys a wider margin, not faster growth. Chevron’s margin lead holds against all three refiners and against Exxon Mobil (XOM), the one peer in Chevron’s own industry. Exxon Mobil trades at 17.0 times earnings with a thinner margin, so against Exxon Mobil you pay less for more. ConocoPhillips (COP), an oil and gas producer and the one peer both cheaper and slower growing than Chevron, earned an even wider 24.7% margin across its whole company. Unlike the three refiners, Chevron produces its own oil and gas, and its plan to produce more is on track so far. In fiscal 2025, the Downstream segment, which runs the refineries, brought in $142 billion of revenue. The Upstream segment, which produces the oil and gas, brought in $88.4 billion. Chevron markets all the crude from its three Venezuela joint ventures, sending most of it to U.S. refineries such as Pascagoula and El Segundo. Management plans to double output from those ventures to roughly 600,000 barrels a day by 2031. It puts the total cost below $20 a barrel, counting both capital spending and operating costs. On the October 30, 2026 call, management said the ventures were on track for their year-end goal of around 300,000 barrels a day of gross production, up 20% over the past 12 months. Chevron’s Permian fields also topped 1 million barrels a day of oil and gas combined for a sixth straight quarter, and management plans to hold output above that level. Owning the oil as well as the refineries may be what buyers are paying for, though most of the Venezuela growth is still years away. Over the four quarters ended September 30, 2026, Chevron earned $27.0 billion in profit. It earned $22.0 billion of that total in fiscal Q2 and Q3 2026 alone. In fiscal Q1 2026, it earned just $2.21 billion. Oil traded as low as $68 and as high as $132 a barrel in the third quarter, management said, and it expects refining margins to stay elevated in the short term, with 10% of the world’s refining capacity offline. You pay about twice a refiner’s multiple for Chevron today. If its profit slips back toward its first-quarter level, that premium would buy neither faster growth nor a wider margin. Management guided a dividend of $1.78 a share for fiscal Q4 2026. It calls growing the dividend its first priority, and Chevron has done so for 39 consecutive years. So if you pay Chevron’s premium, you are betting that it keeps its margin ahead of the refiners’ and gets its Venezuela oil flowing. Over the four quarters taken together, Chevron’s margin stayed ahead of the refiners’, though its quarterly margin swung from 6.8% to 21.2%. The Venezuela growth is still mostly a plan. Chevron’s operating margin in its fiscal Q4 2026 report, expected in January 2027, is the number to watch. Neither oil prices nor project dates are in a Chevron holder’s hands. This is a good reason to spread your money across a group of strong companies rather than holding just one.
